etymology: Reformed-theological term, parallel to the older designation "particular atonement" (and the more polemical TULIP label "limited atonement"). The dictionary prefers definite atonement as the constructive Reformed-confessional name: Christ's atoning work was DEFINITE in its scope (for the elect) and DEFINITE in its accomplishment (effectually saving those for whom He died), not indefinite as Arminian general atonement makes it.
biblical_def: Definite atonement is the Reformed-confessional doctrine that Christ's atoning work on the cross was specifically and effectually for the elect — that He died with the definite purpose and the definite effect of redeeming those whom the Father had given Him. Articulated most fully in John Owen's The Death of Death in the Death of Christ (1647), the doctrine sits at the heart of Reformed soteriology: Father electing, Son atoning, Spirit applying, in perfect Trinitarian unity of purpose for the same elect persons. The biblical evidence: Christ "came to give his life a ransom for many" (Matt 20:28); "I lay down my life for the sheep" (John 10:15); "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Eph 5:25); "He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many" (Isa 53:11). The General Atonement position (Arminian, Wesleyan, modern Evangelical) holds that Christ died for all without distinction in saving intent, with the application contingent on human response. The Reformed position holds that Christ died with definite saving intent and that the application is the effectual fruit of the atoning purchase, secured by the Spirit who applies what Christ accomplished.
webster_summary: Reformed soteriological doctrine that Christ's atoning work was specifically and effectually for the elect; constructive Reformed-confessional name for the same doctrine called "particular atonement" or (more polemically) "limited atonement." Contrasted with general atonement (Arminian, Wesleyan, modern Evangelical default): Christ died for all without distinction in saving intent, application contingent on human response.

corruption_summary: Definite atonement is corrupted when reduced to a polemical TULIP-point against Arminianism rather than received as part of the larger Trinitarian-soteriological frame, when set against the genuine offer of the gospel to all (which the doctrine does not contradict), or when caricatured by detractors as making God indifferent to the non-elect.
corruption_paragraphs: Reduction to TULIP polemic. Definite atonement is often encountered first as the L of TULIP and only as a polemical wedge against Arminianism. The larger Reformed-confessional frame is Trinitarian-soteriological: the Father elects a definite people (Eph 1:4); the Son atones for that definite people (John 10:15; Eph 5:25); the Spirit applies that atonement effectually to the same definite people (Tit 3:5; John 6:44). The three Persons act in perfect unity of purpose for the same elect persons. To meet definite atonement only as "the L" is to miss the Trinitarian frame in which it makes sense.

Misreading as denial of the free offer of the gospel. Hyper-Calvinists deny the free offer of the gospel to all; this is not the Reformed-confessional position and not what definite atonement requires. The historic Reformed-confessional position (Dort, Westminster, LBCF) maintains both definite atonement AND the genuine free offer of the gospel to all without distinction. The atonement was definite in its purchase; the gospel offer is universal in its proclamation; both are biblical, and neither requires the other to be qualified. John Owen himself, the great defender of definite atonement, freely offered Christ to all who would hear him preach.

etymology: Internal-discourse label for the position within Christian discussions of same-sex sexuality that affirms monogamous same-sex sexual unions as biblically permissible and capable of receiving the blessing of the church. Distinguished from Side B (which holds traditional sexual ethics while affirming "gay" as an identity marker) and traditional Reformed-confessional sexual ethics (which rejects both moves).
biblical_def: Side A is the internal-discourse label for the position within Christian conversations about same-sex sexuality that affirms monogamous same-sex sexual unions as biblically permissible and worthy of the church's blessing. It is functionally equivalent to affirming theology (q.v.) but framed within the "Side A / Side B" vocabulary that emerged in the 1990s in Christian gay-Christian online forums (Bridges Across the Divide, the Gay Christian Network). Major representatives include Matthew Vines (Reformation Project), Justin Lee (founder of the Gay Christian Network, 2001), Brandan Robertson, and the institutional shift of mainline denominations. Side A's exegetical moves are the same as affirming theology's: reinterpretation of Lev 18:22 / 20:13 as cultic-context Canaanite condemnations, of Rom 1:26-27 as condemning excess rather than orientation, of 1 Cor 6:9 / 1 Tim 1:10 arsenokoitai as referring to narrower categories than committed same-sex unions. The Reformed-confessional rejection of Side A is the same as the rejection of affirming theology: the plain reading of the canonical text in its Mosaic, prophetic, dominical, and apostolic continuity holds the historic Christian sexual ethic. Distinguished from Side B (q.v.) on the doctrinal question of whether same-sex sexual acts are permissible.

corruption_summary: Side A is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry identifies the label as an internal-discourse marker, names representatives, and rebuts the position on the same biblical grounds as affirming theology generally.
corruption_paragraphs: Same exegetical moves as affirming theology, same rebuttal. Side A is not a doctrinally distinct position from affirming theology; it is the same position framed within the gay-Christian-discourse Side A / Side B vocabulary. The exegetical moves are identical: reframing Leviticus as cultic-context; reframing Romans 1 as excess-condemnation; narrowing 1 Cor 6 / 1 Tim 1 arsenokoitai referents; appealing to Christian-ethics-of-love categories to override specific biblical prohibitions. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal is the same: the plain reading of Lev 18:22 / 20:13, Rom 1:26-27, 1 Cor 6:9-11, 1 Tim 1:9-10, and the apostolic-Lord's appeal to Gen 1:27 + Gen 2:24 at Matt 19:4-6 holds the historic Christian sexual ethic.

Identity-label substitution for repentance-and-faith identity. The Side A / Side B vocabulary itself centers same-sex sexual orientation as a structuring category of Christian identity. The Reformed-confessional reader notes that the apostolic categorization in 1 Cor 6:11 ("such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified") does not retain pre-conversion sexual-identity categories within Christian identity. The gospel produces a new identity in Christ that relativizes the pre-conversion orientation category, whether toward Side A's blessing of the orientation or Side B's preservation of the identity label.

etymology: Internal-discourse label, parallel to Side A, for the position within Christian conversations about same-sex sexuality that holds traditional biblical sexual ethics (no same-sex sexual acts, no same-sex marriage) while affirming "gay" or "same-sex attracted" as a legitimate ongoing identity marker for Christian believers. Originated in the same 1990s Christian gay-Christian forums that produced Side A.
biblical_def: Side B is the position within Christian conversations about same-sex sexuality that holds the traditional biblical sexual ethic (no same-sex sexual acts, no same-sex marriage; celibacy or opposite-sex marriage only) while affirming "gay," "queer," or "same-sex attracted" as a legitimate ongoing identity marker for Christian believers. Major representatives include Wesley Hill (Washed and Waiting, 2010; Spiritual Friendship, 2015), Nate Collins (Revoice founder), Greg Coles (Single, Gay, Christian, 2017), Preston Sprinkle (Center for Faith Sexuality & Gender), and the institutional embodiment in the Revoice Conference (founded 2018). The Reformed-confessional position partially agrees with Side B: celibacy is a legitimate calling (1 Cor 7); same-sex attracted believers who hold the biblical sexual ethic are genuinely Christian. The Reformed-confessional position disagrees with Side B on the identity-labeling: the apostolic pattern in 1 Cor 6:11 ("such were some of you") does not retain pre-conversion sexual-orientation categories within Christian identity; the New Testament knows believers in Christ, not "gay Christians" or "queer Christians." Critics include Robert Gagnon, Owen Strachan, Denny Burk, Voddie Baucham, and the PCA's 2020 Ad Interim Committee Report on Human Sexuality. Side B is theologically more careful than Side A and more pastorally serious than dismissive cultural conservatism; it remains, on the Reformed-confessional reading, a category error in identity formation.

corruption_summary: Side B is itself a contested position that the dictionary engages: partially agreeing on biblical sexual ethics and celibacy, partially rejecting on identity-labeling. The Reformed-confessional reading is that the identity-labeling is a category error even where the underlying sexual ethic is preserved.
corruption_paragraphs: Identity-labeling as category error. Side B's defining move is to preserve "gay," "queer," or "same-sex attracted" as a legitimate ongoing identity marker for the Christian believer while holding the traditional biblical sexual ethic. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: 1 Cor 6:11 does not preserve pre-conversion sexual-orientation categories within Christian identity ("such were some of you: but ye are washed"). 2 Cor 5:17 makes the new-creation status categorical. The PCA's 2020 Ad Interim Committee Report on Human Sexuality articulates the Reformed-Presbyterian position carefully: same-sex attraction can be a continuing pattern of indwelling sin to be mortified, not a redeemable identity to be preserved with a Christian qualifier. The Christian's primary and proper identity is in Christ; the orientation category is not retained.

Pastoral seriousness without category error. The Reformed-confessional reader receives Side B's contribution honestly. Wesley Hill's Washed and Waiting takes celibacy and biblical sexual ethics with more seriousness than much of dismissive cultural conservatism does, and treats same-sex attracted believers as fellow saints rather than as cultural enemies. The pastoral seriousness is recognized and commended. The category error in identity formation is rejected. Both can be done in the same sentence: honor the brother's biblical commitments; refuse the identity grammar that names his besetting sin as part of his Christian self-description.

etymology: Twenty-first ecumenical council of the Roman Catholic Church, convened by Pope John XXIII (1962) and concluded under Pope Paul VI (1965). Held in four sessions at the Vatican; produced sixteen documents that reoriented modern Roman Catholic practice and ecumenical posture. Distinct from the First Vatican Council (1869-70, which defined papal infallibility).
biblical_def: The Second Vatican Council (1962-1965) was the twenty-first ecumenical council of the Roman Catholic Church and the most consequential modern reorientation of Roman Catholic practice and ecumenical posture. Convened by Pope John XXIII (October 1962); concluded under Pope Paul VI (December 1965); produced sixteen documents including four constitutions (Sacrosanctum Concilium on the liturgy; Lumen Gentium on the church; Dei Verbum on revelation; Gaudium et Spes on the church in the modern world). The major shifts: the Mass translated into vernacular languages (replacing the Latin Tridentine Rite as the standard); reorientation of the priest to face the congregation; expanded ecumenical openness toward Protestants (renamed "separated brethren") and Eastern Orthodox; reaffirmation of papal authority alongside collegial-episcopal governance; expanded religious-liberty teaching (Dignitatis Humanae); and a general aggiornamento ("updating") of Roman Catholic engagement with modernity. The Reformed-confessional engagement is layered: Vatican II's softened polemic toward Protestants is welcomed where it allows fellowship and conversation; Vatican II's reaffirmation of the historic Tridentine doctrinal positions (transubstantiation, papal authority, treasury of merit, Marian dogmas, sacramental system) means the substantive doctrinal corruptions the Reformation rejected remain in place. Roman Catholic apologists sometimes argue that Vatican II resolved the Reformation tensions; the Reformed-confessional reader notes that the Trent definitions Vatican II reaffirmed are themselves the substance of the Reformation rejection.

corruption_summary: Vatican II is itself an event the dictionary names. The Reformed-confessional engagement welcomes the softened polemic toward Protestants while noting that the Tridentine doctrinal substance Vatican II reaffirmed is itself the substance of what the Reformation rejected.
corruption_paragraphs: Apparent rapprochement without doctrinal change. Modern Roman Catholic apologists sometimes argue that Vatican II resolved the substantive Reformation tensions: the Mass is now in the vernacular (which was a Reformation concern); Protestants are called "separated brethren" rather than heretics; the laity is encouraged to read Scripture; ecumenical dialogue is celebrated. These shifts are real and the Reformed-confessional reader welcomes them where they allow fellowship and conversation. But the doctrinal substance the Reformation rejected was specifically: transubstantiation, papal infallibility and universal jurisdiction, the treasury of merit and indulgences, purgatory, the Marian dogmas (Immaculate Conception 1854, Bodily Assumption 1950), denial of sola Scriptura, denial of sola fide. Each of these was reaffirmed at Trent (1545-1563) and reaffirmed (not modified) at Vatican II. The apparent rapprochement is procedural, not substantive.

Lumen Gentium's ecclesiology specifically. The Vatican II constitution on the church (Lumen Gentium, 1964) provides the most-cited evidence for ecumenical opening: it teaches that the church of Christ "subsists in" the Roman Catholic Church (LG 8) while elements of grace and truth exist outside it. Roman Catholic ecumenists read this as a softening of the historic "extra ecclesiam nulla salus" (no salvation outside the church). The Reformed-confessional reader notes the limits: LG 14 still teaches that those who know the Roman Catholic Church is necessary for salvation cannot be saved if they refuse to enter or remain in it; LG 22-25 reaffirms full papal authority over the church universal; and the post-Vatican II papacy (John Paul II, Benedict XVI) explicitly maintained that "subsists in" does not mean "is equivalent to" the Roman Catholic Church's identity with the church of Christ. The opening is real and procedural; the doctrinal substance of Roman ecclesiology remains.

etymology: Term used by both internal advocates and external critics to label various 20th- and 21st-century Christian programs for explicit Christian political-cultural "dominion." Internally distinguishable into several distinct positions: Christian Reconstructionism / Theonomy (Rushdoony, Bahnsen, North); the Seven Mountains Mandate (Wallnau, NAR-adjacent); broader Christian-influence-in-culture programs (sometimes loosely called "dominionist" by critics).
biblical_def: Dominionism is the loosely-used label for various 20th- and 21st-century Christian programs that argue for explicit Christian dominion or rule over public-cultural-political life. It is critical to distinguish several distinct positions the label is often applied to: (1) Christian Reconstructionism / Theonomy — R.J. Rushdoony (The Institutes of Biblical Law, 1973), Greg Bahnsen, Gary North, and the broader Chalcedon Foundation tradition, which argues that the Mosaic civil law (including its penalties) should be applied to modern civil states under Christian magistracy. (2) The Seven Mountains Mandate — Lance Wallnau, Loren Cunningham, and NAR-adjacent figures, which calls Christians to take over the seven "mountains" of cultural influence (religion, family, education, government, media, arts, business) ahead of Christ's return. (3) Broader Christian-influence-in-culture programs — Kuyperian neo-Calvinism, the Christian Right of the 1980s, James Dobson / Focus on the Family, the broader Christian-engagement-with-politics conversation. The Reformed-confessional engagement varies sharply: positions (1) and (2) are largely rejected by mainstream confessional Reformed (LBCF, Westminster, OPC, PCA, ARP); position (3) is internal to mainstream Reformed conversation. The biblical dominion mandate of Gen 1:28 ("Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion") is a creational mandate for human stewardship of the world under God, not a mandate for any specific political-theological program. The label "dominionism" should be used with care.
webster_summary: Loosely-used label for 20th-21st century Christian political-cultural programs; distinguishable into Christian Reconstructionism / Theonomy (Rushdoony, Bahnsen), Seven Mountains Mandate (Wallnau, NAR-adjacent), and broader Christian-influence programs; Gen 1:28 dominion mandate is creational stewardship not specific political program.

Mainstream Reformed-confessional reception: (1) and (2) largely rejected by LBCF / Westminster / OPC / PCA / ARP; (3) internal to mainstream Reformed conversation.
Distinguished from the biblical dominion mandate (Gen 1:28), which is creational stewardship of the world under God, not a specific political-theological program.

corruption_summary: Dominionism as a category is variously applied. The dictionary distinguishes biblical dominion mandate (Gen 1:28 creational stewardship) from specific political-theological programs (Christian Reconstructionism / Theonomy; Seven Mountains Mandate), and engages each program by name on its biblical-doctrinal merits.
corruption_paragraphs: Christian Reconstructionism / Theonomy specifically. Rushdoony's Institutes of Biblical Law (1973) argues that the Mosaic civil law (including capital sanctions for idolatry, blasphemy, Sabbath-breaking, etc.) should be applied to modern civil states under Christian magistracy. Bahnsen's Theonomy in Christian Ethics (1977) systematized the position. Mainstream Reformed-confessional rejection: Westminster Confession 19:4 teaches that the judicial / civil laws of Israel expired with Israel as a body politic ("not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require"); the LBCF follows substantively the same position; the mainstream Reformed-Presbyterian and Reformed-Baptist tradition rejects theonomy on confessional grounds. Theonomy remains a minority Reformed position with serious advocates but is not the mainstream Reformed-confessional standard.

Seven Mountains Mandate specifically. Lance Wallnau and Loren Cunningham's Seven Mountains Mandate is distinct from theonomy and is more NAR-adjacent: it calls believers to take over the seven "mountains" of cultural influence (religion, family, education, government, media, arts, business) as preparation for Christ's return. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the New Testament eschatology of the kingdom is not that the church accomplishes Christ's reign by taking the mountains of culture, but that Christ Himself returns to consummate the kingdom He has already inaugurated (1 Cor 15:24-28; Rev 19-22). The Seven Mountains program collapses inaugurated-not-yet-consummated eschatology into a triumphalist program of cultural conquest. Distinct from Kuyperian neo-Calvinism's longer-form engagement with culture, which works within the inaugurated-not-yet frame.

etymology: Late-1990s and early-2000s American Christian movement loosely associated with the Emergent Village network (Brian McLaren, Doug Pagitt, Tony Jones), proposing a postmodern reframing of evangelical Christianity for the "emerging" postmodern generation. Distinct from but overlapping with the related "emergent church" (q.v.) label.
biblical_def: The Emerging Church was a late-1990s through early-2010s American Christian movement that proposed a postmodern reframing of evangelical Christianity for what its leaders called the "emerging" postmodern cultural generation. Major representatives: Brian McLaren (A New Kind of Christian, 2001; A Generous Orthodoxy, 2004; A New Kind of Christianity, 2010); Doug Pagitt (Solomon's Porch, Minneapolis); Tony Jones (Emergent Village); Rob Bell (Mars Hill Bible Church, Grand Rapids; Love Wins, 2011). Key features: skepticism toward propositional doctrine and systematic theology; preference for narrative theology and story-based preaching; suspicion of evangelical certainty as a remnant of modernism; openness to postmodern epistemology and to ecumenical-Roman-Catholic-Orthodox sources; gradual softening on biblical sexuality, eschatology, atonement theory, and (in Bell's case) the doctrine of hell. The movement reached its public peak around 2005-2010 and effectively dissolved or transformed by 2015 into either (a) full progressive Christianity (McLaren, Pagitt; the Wild Goose Festival orbit) or (b) the broader exvangelical / deconstruction movement (Bell, Rachel Held Evans). The Reformed-confessional engagement: the Emerging Church's epistemological-postmodern reframing of biblical authority was rebutted in real time by D.A. Carson (Becoming Conversant with the Emerging Church, 2005), Mark Driscoll's harder break, and Kevin DeYoung & Ted Kluck (Why We're Not Emergent, 2008). The dictionary names the movement as the late-1990s-through-2010s evangelical-adjacent transition into what became progressive Christianity.

corruption_summary: The Emerging Church is itself a corruption pattern being named: the late-1990s-through-2010s evangelical-adjacent transition that softened propositional doctrine, biblical authority, and historic Christian eschatology in the name of postmodern engagement, and that effectively dissolved into progressive Christianity or the deconstruction movement.
corruption_paragraphs: Postmodern epistemology as biblical authority-softener. The Emerging Church's central move was epistemological: treating evangelical certainty about biblical authority, propositional doctrine, and systematic theology as a remnant of modernist Enlightenment confidence that the postmodern generation could no longer share. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: biblical authority is not derived from modernist epistemological confidence; it derives from God's self-revelation in inspired Scripture (2 Tim 3:16). The postmodern question ("can you really know?") is the same question the serpent asked in Eden ("Yea, hath God said?" Gen 3:1). The Reformed-confessional answer is the same as the apostolic answer: yes, God has spoken; the prophetic Word is more sure (2 Pet 1:19); the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3).

Trajectory from softening to dissolution. The Emerging Church's leaders did not stop at the postmodern epistemological move; they progressively softened on biblical sexuality (McLaren, Bell, eventually all major figures), on the doctrine of hell (Bell's Love Wins, 2011), on substitutionary penal atonement (McLaren's A New Kind of Christianity, 2010), and ultimately on the gospel itself. By 2015 the movement had effectively dissolved into either full progressive Christianity or the broader exvangelical / deconstruction movement. The trajectory confirms what the Reformed-confessional critics warned in real time: the postmodern epistemological softening was not stable; once the "you can't really know" move was granted, the doctrinal substance progressively eroded along predictable lines. The dictionary names this trajectory plainly.

etymology: Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber (1934-1997) at Fuller Theological Seminary's MC510 course ("Signs, Wonders, and Church Growth," 1982-1986) and at the Vineyard Christian Fellowship network. The phrase "signs and wonders" comes from Acts 2:43 et al., redeployed by Wimber and successors as a program for present-day Spirit-empowered ministry beyond the apostolic age.
biblical_def: The Signs and Wonders Movement is the Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber (1934-1997) at Fuller Theological Seminary in the early 1980s and centered on the Vineyard Christian Fellowship network. Wimber taught Fuller's controversial MC510 course ("Signs, Wonders, and Church Growth," 1982-1986), proposing that the present-day church should expect and pursue the signs and wonders of the apostolic age — healings, prophetic words, deliverance, sometimes raisings — as ordinary marks of Spirit-empowered ministry. The movement spread through the Vineyard network, the Toronto Blessing (1994), the Brownsville Revival (1995), and into the contemporary Bethel Church (Bill Johnson, Redding, CA) and IHOP (Mike Bickle, Kansas City) networks. Theological distinctives: present-day continuation of apostolic-age sign gifts; signs and wonders as evangelistic norm rather than apostolic accreditation; "power evangelism" over "programmatic evangelism"; expectation that physical healings should be sought and often occur in normal Christian ministry. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal is cessationist: the apostolic sign gifts (healings, miracles, prophetic word, tongues-as-foreign-language) served to accredit the apostolic foundation of the church (Heb 2:3-4; 2 Cor 12:12 "the signs of an apostle") and ceased with the close of the apostolic era and the closing of the canon (1 Cor 13:8-10). Modern claims to apostolic-level signs and wonders are tested by Scripture; documented patterns of unfulfilled prophecy, manipulated "healing", and theological drift (especially at Bethel and IHOP) confirm the cessationist concern.

corruption_summary: The Signs and Wonders Movement is itself the corruption pattern being named: the late-20th-century charismatic-evangelical movement claiming present-day continuation of apostolic-age sign gifts as ordinary ministry, rebutted from cessationist Reformed-confessional grounds.
corruption_paragraphs: Apostolic-accreditation framing collapsed into ordinary-ministry framing. The New Testament data on signs and wonders has a clear pattern: signs and wonders accredited the apostolic foundation of the church (Heb 2:3-4 "confirmed unto us by them that heard him... with signs and wonders"; 2 Cor 12:12 "the signs of an apostle... in signs and wonders"); they served the unique foundational moment when the apostolic message was being delivered without a closed New Testament canon to confirm it. The Reformed-confessional cessationist position holds that these sign gifts ceased with the close of the apostolic era because their function (accreditation of the apostolic foundation) was completed. The Signs and Wonders Movement collapses the foundational-accreditation function into an ordinary-ministry function, treating apostolic-level miracles as the normal expectation of every Spirit-filled congregation. The collapse is not biblical.

Empirical pattern of unfulfilled prophecy and manipulated "healing". The Signs and Wonders Movement's institutional descendants (Bethel, IHOP, the broader Vineyard) have a documented pattern of (a) prophetic words that did not come to pass (with subsequent revision or quiet abandonment), (b) "healings" that were not actual healings (medical follow-up confirms no change), and (c) theological drift on Christ's nature (Bill Johnson's Christology of Christ ministering as a man in right relationship with God), the closed canon, and biblical authority. The Reformed-confessional reader notes that Deut 13:1-3 specifically warns against following signs-and-wonders teachers who turn the people away from the LORD even when their signs come to pass; the test of a movement is conformity to Scripture, not the impressiveness of its phenomena. The empirical record of the Signs and Wonders Movement confirms what the cessationist position predicted on biblical grounds.

etymology: Sociological-category label that emerged in late-20th-century American religious surveys (Princeton Religion Research Center; Pew Research) for respondents who affirmed personal spiritual practice or belief while rejecting affiliation with organized religion. By the 2010s SBNR had become one of the fastest-growing self-identification categories in American religious demographics.
biblical_def: Spiritual But Not Religious (SBNR) is the sociological-category label for the rapidly growing American demographic that affirms personal spiritual practice or belief while rejecting affiliation with organized religion. The Pew Research Center documented SBNR's growth from roughly 19% of American adults in 2012 to roughly 27% by 2017; the broader "Nones" (religiously unaffiliated) reached 28% by 2021. SBNR is not a single belief system but a self-identification pattern combining various elements: vague theistic or pantheistic belief; meditation, yoga, or other mind-body practice; appreciation of "spiritual" literature (Rumi, Tolle, etc.); explicit rejection of institutional religious membership; suspicion of organized religion as hypocritical, hierarchical, or politically compromised. From the Reformed-confessional standpoint, SBNR represents the late-modern dechristianization of American culture combined with a continuing felt-need for transcendence: the felt-need is real (Rom 1:19-20 the knowledge of God impressed on every human heart), the spiritual practices substituted for biblical worship are insufficient, and the rejection of organized religion bypasses the New Testament category of the local church (Heb 10:25; 1 Tim 3:15). Biblical worship is not a generic spiritual experience; it is the corporate, ordinance-using, Word-and-Spirit fellowship of the gathered local church under qualified elder oversight. SBNR is a sociological symptom of late-modern American dechristianization; the Reformed-confessional response is renewed local-church recovery and re-evangelization, not capitulation to the SBNR frame.

corruption_summary: SBNR is itself a sociological pattern that the dictionary names: late-modern American dechristianization combined with continuing felt-need for transcendence; substitutes generic personal practice for biblical local-church worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Felt-need for transcendence is real; the SBNR answer is insufficient. Romans 1:19-20 teaches that the knowledge of God is impressed on every human heart through creation, leaving every person without excuse. The SBNR demographic's continuing felt-need for transcendence is consistent with Rom 1's account: the knowledge of God cannot be fully suppressed, even by late-modern dechristianization. But the substitute practices (yoga, meditation, "spiritual" reading, vague pantheism) are insufficient to address the felt-need because the felt-need is for the LIVING GOD — the God who has spoken in His Word, who is approached only through Christ the Mediator, and who has appointed the local church as the ordinary means of grace. The SBNR substitute is honored as evidence that the felt-need is real; it is rebutted as insufficient on its merits.

Rejection of organized religion bypasses the local church. SBNR's rejection of "organized religion" is often grounded in real criticisms of religious institutions: hypocrisy, hierarchical abuse, political compromise, cold formalism. The Reformed-confessional reader takes the criticisms seriously where they are accurate (the church is always being reformed, semper reformanda). But the rejection of organized religion as such bypasses the New Testament category of the local church: a Spirit-gathered assembly of redeemed believers under qualified elder oversight, using the ordinances Christ appointed, hearing the Word preached, and walking in mutual covenant fellowship (Heb 10:25; 1 Tim 3:15; Acts 2:42-47). Christ did not appoint individualized private spirituality; He appointed His church. SBNR's substitute cannot deliver what only the church can: the ordinary means of grace by which God's people are nourished into eternal life.

etymology: Mid-20th-century American Protestant missiology and church-management movement initiated by Donald McGavran (The Bridges of God, 1955; Understanding Church Growth, 1970) at Fuller Theological Seminary's School of World Mission. Developed in the 1980s-90s by C. Peter Wagner (Fuller missiologist) and applied to North American church-planting and church-management by Rick Warren (Saddleback Church) and Bill Hybels (Willow Creek Community Church).
biblical_def: The Church Growth Movement is the mid-20th-century American Protestant missiology-and-management movement that applied sociological and managerial techniques to evangelical church planting and church growth. Initiated by Donald McGavran (The Bridges of God, 1955; Understanding Church Growth, 1970) at Fuller Seminary's School of World Mission; developed institutionally by C. Peter Wagner (Fuller missiologist, 1971-1999); applied to North American church-planting and management most prominently by Rick Warren (Saddleback Church; The Purpose-Driven Church, 1995) and Bill Hybels (Willow Creek Community Church; the Willow Creek Association of seeker-sensitive megachurches). Theological-methodological distinctives: church growth as the primary metric of church health; sociological-demographic analysis to identify target populations (the "homogeneous unit principle" in McGavran); seeker-sensitive worship designed to remove cultural barriers for unchurched attenders; pragmatic adoption of cultural forms (music, preaching style, programming) to maximize church-attendance growth; explicit borrowing from business-management theory (Drucker; later Peter Senge). The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the New Testament metric of church health is faithfulness to apostolic doctrine, ordinances, and discipline (Acts 2:42; 1 Tim 3:15), not numerical-attendance growth; the seeker-sensitive removal of cultural barriers often removes biblical-doctrinal substance (preaching of repentance, judgment, the cross, the wrath of God) along with the cultural form; and the pragmatic adoption of business-management methods substitutes the Drucker-Senge ecclesiology for biblical ecclesiology.
webster_summary: Mid-20th-century American Protestant missiology-and-management movement initiated by McGavran (Fuller, 1955-70); developed by Wagner; applied to North American churches by Warren (Saddleback, Purpose-Driven, 1995) and Hybels (Willow Creek); rebutted on biblical-ecclesiology grounds (church health = doctrinal faithfulness, not numerical growth).

corruption_summary: The Church Growth Movement is itself a methodological pattern that the dictionary names: mid-20th-century American Protestant missiology-and-management that subordinated biblical ecclesiology to sociological-demographic and business-management techniques in pursuit of numerical growth.
corruption_paragraphs: Numerical growth as primary metric. The Church Growth Movement's defining methodological move is to make numerical attendance growth the primary metric of church health and pastoral success. The New Testament metric is different: doctrinal faithfulness to the apostolic teaching, ordinances, and discipline (Acts 2:42; 1 Tim 3:15; 2 Tim 4:1-4 the charge to Timothy is to preach the Word, not to grow the congregation). A faithful Reformed-confessional pulpit may produce a numerically smaller congregation than an unfaithful seeker-sensitive pulpit, and the smaller faithful church is the one Christ commends in Rev 2-3, not the larger compromised church. The metric substitution is the corruption.

Seeker-sensitive removal of biblical-doctrinal substance. The Church Growth Movement's secondary methodological move is to remove cultural barriers between the unchurched seeker and the church's worship gathering. In practice this has often meant removing biblical-doctrinal substance along with the cultural barrier: preaching of repentance, judgment, the cross, the wrath of God, sin, and hell is muted because it is "off-putting" to seekers. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the gospel itself is the offense that the seeker-sensitive method removes (1 Cor 1:18-25). To remove the offense is to remove the gospel. Hybels himself acknowledged in 2007 (the Reveal Survey) that Willow Creek's seeker-sensitive program had not produced disciples of Christ; the empirical confession confirms what the Reformed-confessional critique had said in principle.

etymology: Classical Reformed-theological term for God's eternal, unconditional, sovereign, and unchangeable purpose by which He has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass. Standard articulation in Westminster Confession of Faith chapter 3 ("Of God's Eternal Decree") and parallel 1689 LBCF chapter 3 (same title). Singular "decree" (rather than plural "decrees") emphasizes the unity of God's one comprehensive purpose; the plural can be used for the differentiated aspects.
biblical_def: The decree of God is the classical Reformed-theological doctrine that God has from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordained whatsoever comes to pass (WCF 3:1; LBCF 3:1, the language is identical in the two confessions on this point). The doctrine articulates God's relation to all of creation, providence, and salvation in the categories of eternal purpose. Major components articulated in the Reformed confessions: (1) the decree is from all eternity, not in time; (2) it proceeds from God's wise and holy counsel, not from external compulsion or contingency; (3) it is free, not constrained by creaturely will or merit; (4) it is unchangeable, not subject to revision; (5) it comprehends whatsoever comes to pass, both what God effectively does and what He permits secondary causes to do (without God being the author of sin, WCF 3:1 / LBCF 3:1); (6) it includes the gracious election of some to everlasting life through Christ and the just passing-by of others (the doctrine of election and reprobation, WCF 3:3-8 / LBCF 3:3-7); (7) it is the ground of all divine action in creation, providence, and salvation. The biblical foundation: Eph 1:11 ("worketh all things after the counsel of his own will"); Isa 46:10 ("My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure"); Acts 4:27-28 (Christ's crucifixion accomplished according to the predetermined counsel); Rom 9 (the potter and clay; election and reprobation); Rom 11:33-36 (the depth of God's unsearchable judgments).
webster_summary: Classical Reformed-theological doctrine of God's eternal, free, unchangeable, sovereign purpose by which He has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass; articulated WCF / LBCF 3:1; biblical foundation Eph 1:11, Isa 46:10, Acts 4:27-28, Rom 9, Rom 11:33-36.
webster_full: DECREE OF GOD, noun phrase. Classical Reformed-theological doctrine.
Standard articulation: Westminster Confession of Faith chapter 3 ("Of God's Eternal Decree"); 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith chapter 3 (identical language in 3:1).
Components: from all eternity; by God's wise and holy counsel; free; unchangeable; comprehends whatsoever comes to pass; includes election and reprobation; is the ground of all divine action.
Singular "decree" emphasizes unity of God's one comprehensive purpose; plural "decrees" can name differentiated aspects.
Biblical foundation: Eph 1:11; Isa 46:10; Acts 4:27-28; Rom 9; Rom 11:33-36.
scriptures: Ephesians 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will.
Isaiah 46:9-10

Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me, Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.

For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together, For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.
Romans 11:33-36

O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of God's eternal decree is corrupted when reduced to a polemical wedge against Arminianism, when made the ground for human passivity or fatalism, when used to make God the author of sin (which the Reformed confessions explicitly deny), or when collapsed into modern process-theology / Open-Theism alternatives that deny the doctrine altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Fatalism misreading. The doctrine of the decree is sometimes received with horror as if it produced fatalism ("if God has decreed everything, then human action does not matter; we are puppets"). The Reformed confessions explicitly reject this inference. WCF 3:1 / LBCF 3:1 teaches that God's decree is the ground of creaturely action, not the negation of it: "Yet so, as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established." The decree is the ground of meaningful human action because it gives the action its actual existence and its place in God's purpose; meaningful action presupposes the decree, not contradicts it. The Reformed pastoral application is the opposite of fatalism: confidence to act faithfully because the LORD has ordered the times and the outcomes.

Process-theology and Open-Theism denial. The 20th-century alternatives that deny the classical doctrine of the decree are process theology (Whitehead, Hartshorne, Cobb) and Open Theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders). Both teach that the future is at least partly open even to God, that God does not exhaustively foreknow free creaturely decisions, and that history therefore unfolds with genuine contingency that God responds to rather than ordains. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: Eph 1:11 makes the decree exhaustive ("worketh ALL THINGS after the counsel of his own will"); Isa 46:10 makes the decree future-comprehending ("declaring the end from the beginning"); Acts 4:27-28 makes the decree compatible with creaturely action (Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and Israel did what they did, and God's counsel determined it). The classical decree is the biblical doctrine; the open-theistic alternative is a different God.
roots_summary: Classical Reformed-theological doctrine of God's eternal, free, unchangeable, sovereign purpose by which He has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass; WCF / LBCF 3:1; biblical foundation Eph 1:11, Isa 46:10, Acts 4:27-28, Rom 9, Rom 11:33-36.
roots_lines: Classical Reformed-theological doctrine; standard articulation in WCF chapter 3 and LBCF chapter 3 (identical language in 3:1)
Components: eternal; from God's wise and holy counsel; free; unchangeable; comprehensive; includes election and reprobation; ground of all divine action

Compatibilist frame: WCF 3:1 / LBCF 3:1 explicitly maintains that God is not the author of sin, the will of the creature is not violated, and the liberty or contingency of secondary causes is not taken away, but rather established

Major systematic-theological treatments: Francis Turretin (Institutes of Elenctic Theology, vol. 1, on the decree); Wilhelmus à Brakel (The Christian's Reasonable Service); Charles Hodge (Systematic Theology, vol. 1); Louis Berkhof (Systematic Theology, on the decree)
20th-century deniers: Process theology (Whitehead, Hartshorne, Cobb); Open Theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders); rebutted on Eph 1:11, Isa 46:10, Acts 4:27-28
usage: Decree of God — the classical Reformed-theological doctrine of God's eternal sovereign purpose; WCF / LBCF chapter 3.
Worketh all things after the counsel of his own will (Eph 1:11) — the apostolic axiom of the doctrine.
Pastoral application: not fatalism but confidence to act faithfully because the LORD has ordered the times and the outcomes.
